sentences.text: The name Megapaloelodus merges the Greek word for 'great' with a misspelling of Palaelodus, which translates to 'ancient inhabitant of marshes'.
Scientists chose this name because the initial remains discovered were physically larger than those of Palaelodus goliath.
This animal resembled flamingos from the Palaelodus group but possessed a much greater body size.
Unlike modern flamingos, Megapaloelodus likely possessed a beak that was less curved.
The species M. peiranoi featured a short, robust forearm rather than the elongated limb seen in Palaelodus and living flamingos.
A distinct feature of the genus is a pronounced tubercle on the trochlea, appearing as a rounded point on the upper rim of the bone where it connects to carpal bones.
The profile of the tibiotarsus shows a deep, rounded notch paired with a large, hooked process.
Members of this genus were typically larger than their relatives in the genus Palaelodus.
They likely inhabited lakes that were sometimes highly saline or brackish.
Fossils from France indicate that M. goliath lived in a brackish lake environment experiencing cyclical wet and dry periods.
American paleontologist Alden H. Miller established the genus Megapaloelodus in 1944 using fossils recovered from South Dakota.
In 1950, Loye H. Miller assigned a fragment of a tibiotarsus and an ulna from late Miocene California to the species M. connectens.
Pierce Brodkorb later described the species M. opsigonus from Juntura, Oregon.
Jacques Cheneval moved the species Palaelodus goliath into the genus Megapaloelodus in 1983.
The species M. peiranoi was formally described in 2009 based on specimens unearthed in Argentina.
Researchers propose that Megapaloelodus might have been able to lock its legs while standing.
A colleague suggested that notches on the leg bones permitted the bird to secure its legs in an upright sleeping posture.
This animal shared its habitat with the genera Palaelodus and Harrisonavis.
The genus Megapaloelodus was previously synonymized with the misspelled name Megapalaelodus.
It belongs to the family Palaelodidae, a group that links modern flamingos and grebes.
Studies indicate that the Palaelodidae family forms a sister group to the flamingo family Phoenicopteridae.
The species M. peiranoi is hypothesized to be the most basal member of the genus Megapaloelodus.
Megapaloelodus lived from the Late Oligocene to the Early Pliocene.
Fossils are primarily found in Miocene deposits across America, although the species M. goliath was discovered in Europe.
M. goliath is the earliest known species of Megapaloelodus, existing from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene, and it is the only named species found outside the Americas.
The species M. goliath lived in the Early Miocene in France.
The species M. opsigonus was found in the Pliocene Juntura Formation in Oregon.
The species name M. opsigonus means 'born in a later age', referring to its appearance during the Pliocene.
The species M. peiranoi was discovered in the Late Miocene Andalhualá Formation of Argentina.
The species M. opsigonus lived in the Pliocene in the United States.
Palaelodus is the only known palaelodid with preserved skull material, showing a straight bill unlike derived flamingos.
In 2002, Jiří Mlíkovský suggested that the genus Megapaloelodus should be synonymized with Palaelodus.
Other authors consider this suggestion to be premature and criticize this taxonomic treatment.
